passages.original: καί σʼ ὦ νεανίσχʼ ὅστις εἶ, κατʼ Αἰσχύλον
passages.english: And you, young man, whoever you are, in the manner of Aeschylus,
passages.notes: A single verse, incomplete in sense; the sentence continues beyond the passage. "In the manner of Aeschylus" (κατ' Αἰσχύλον) introduces a question or quotation in Aeschylean style.

passages.original: ὁ δʼ αὖ Θέογνις ψυχρὸς ὢν ψυχρῶς ποιεῖ.
passages.english: And Theognis, in turn, being frigid, writes frigidly.
passages.notes: Theognis here is the tragic poet mocked by Aristophanes for 'frigidity' (psychros, 'cold', used of flat, lifeless style), not the elegiac poet of Megara.

passages.english: Oh, thrice-wretched me, how ruined is Euripides!
passages.notes: Could also be rendered as a statement: "Euripides is utterly ruined." τρισκακοδαίμων may refer to Euripides himself ("thrice-wretched Euripides") rather than to the speaker.

passages.english: We do, at least. And then are we angry with Euripides,
passages.notes: A single verse, incomplete in sense. The final clause may be a question ("and then do we get angry with Euripides…?") continuing into the next line.
